title: How to Handle Zendrop Stockouts Without Losing the Sale
excerpt: A sold-out variant does not have to become a refund. This workflow shows how to spot stockouts early, message the delay honestly, and protect repeat purchase rate.
body: Every dropshipping store hits the same wall eventually: a product sells, the supplier is out of stock, and the only tool most founders reach for is the refund button. A stockout is not a rare event to be handled case by case. It is a predictable operating condition, and the stores that keep their repeat purchase rate treat it as a workflow with rules rather than a daily crisis. The cost is never just the order value. You also lose the ad spend that brought the customer in, the delivery window you promised, and often the review.

Make stockouts visible before the customer notices them. Pull your top fifty SKUs by revenue each morning and check availability on each variant, not just the parent product. Variants are where stockouts hide, because a listing can look perfectly healthy while the size or colour that drives most of your sales is gone. Keep a simple sheet with three columns: last checked date, current status, and the action you took. Ten minutes a day across fifty SKUs catches most problems while the affected volume is still small.

Decide in advance what happens when a SKU goes dark, based on the revenue it carries. For your top tier, arrange a backup source before you need one and keep a unit of buffer stock if cash flow allows. For the middle tier, map each product to an acceptable substitute variant and confirm the substitution still clears your margin floor after shipping. For the long tail, take the listing down the same day. Writing them down removes the judgement call when you are least able to make one calmly.

The message you send matters more than the stockout itself. Send one email within twenty four hours, state the actual delay in days rather than a vague soon, and give the customer two concrete choices: wait, or switch to a named alternative that ships now. Add a small credit only if the delay crosses your own threshold. Customers accept delays far more readily than silence, and a single honest email turns a likely refund into a deferred delivery in most cases. The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist of supplier platforms with ratings and pricing.

Set a backorder ceiling for every delivery promise you advertise. If you sell a five to eight day window, a fourteen day backorder is a broken promise no matter how politely it is delivered. Pick a number, for most stores it sits between seven and ten days, and let the system refund automatically once the order passes it. Automation removes the temptation to let an order drift another week hoping the supplier recovers. Log every automatic refund with the supplier name attached so the pattern becomes visible.

Finally, review the log monthly instead of reacting SKU by SKU. A supplier that appears three times in a quarter is costing you more in refunds and support time than the margin it appears to save. Move that volume to a source with a better fill rate, even at a slightly higher unit cost, and rerun your landed margin on the new rate.
